column5: Unit 1.1: I can greet someone, say goodbye, and recognize Spanish cognates while pronouncing the five vowels clearly.
column8: Goal: I can greet someone, say goodbye, and recognize Spanish cognates while pronouncing the five vowels clearly. Key phrases: Hola / Adiós / Buenos días / ¿Cómo estás? / la información. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column14: Unit 2.1: I can greet people at different times of day, say hello informally, ask how someone is, and say goodbye politely.
column17: Goal: I can greet people at different times of day, say hello informally, ask how someone is, and say goodbye politely. Key phrases: Buenos días / ¿Qué tal? / ¿Cómo estás? / Bien, gracias / Hasta luego. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column23: Unit 3.1: I can say who I am and who others are using subject pronouns and the verb ser, singular and plural.
column26: Goal: I can say who I am and who others are using subject pronouns and the verb ser, singular and plural. Key phrases: Yo soy / Tú eres / Ella es / Nosotros somos / Ustedes son. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column32: Unit 4.1: I can use regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs and ir in the present to talk about what people do.
column35: Goal: I can use regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs and ir in the present to talk about what people do. Key phrases: Hablo / Como / Vivo / Voy a la tienda / Ellos trabajan. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column41: Unit 5.1: I can use estar to say where and how someone is, and choose ser or estar for events, time, material and origin.
column44: Goal: I can use estar to say where and how someone is, and choose ser or estar for events, time, material and origin. Key phrases: Estoy cansado / Está en casa / Es de madera / La fiesta es en mi casa / Son las cinco. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column50: Unit 6.1: I can use stem-changing verbs e to ie, o to ue and e to i in real sentences.
column53: Goal: I can use stem-changing verbs e to ie, o to ue and e to i in real sentences. Key phrases: Quiero / Puedo / Pido / Duermo / Prefiero. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column59: Unit 7.1: I can say what I like and dislike using gustar with nouns and infinitives, and show degrees of liking.
column62: Goal: I can say what I like and dislike using gustar with nouns and infinitives, and show degrees of liking. Key phrases: Me gusta... / No me gusta... / Me encanta cantar / Odio madrugar / A mí me gusta. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column68: Unit 8.1: I can use reflexive verbs in all persons, place pronouns with infinitives and gerunds, and express wishes with ojalá and espero que.
column71: Goal: I can use reflexive verbs in all persons, place pronouns with infinitives and gerunds, and express wishes with ojalá and espero que. Key phrases: Me levanto / Voy a lavarme / Estoy bañándome / Lo estoy haciendo / Ojalá que.... Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column77: Unit 9.1: I can recognize and form the preterite of regular verbs and place accent marks on endings like habló.
column80: Goal: I can recognize and form the preterite of regular verbs and place accent marks on endings like habló. Key phrases: Ayer / Anoche / Hablé / Comió / Vivieron. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column86: Unit 10.1: I can use j-stem and stem-changing preterites, preterites of leer and oír, and meaning changes with saber and conocer.
column89: Goal: I can use j-stem and stem-changing preterites, preterites of leer and oír, and meaning changes with saber and conocer. Key phrases: Dijo / Trajo / Pidió / Leyó / Supe. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column95: Unit 11.1: I can form past participles and use the present perfect to say what I have done, with questions and negatives.
column98: Goal: I can form past participles and use the present perfect to say what I have done, with questions and negatives. Key phrases: He comido / Has visto / Ha hecho / No he terminado / ¿Has estado...?. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column104: Unit 12.1: I can distinguish completed and ongoing past actions and tell stories with interruptions and background.
column107: Goal: I can distinguish completed and ongoing past actions and tell stories with interruptions and background. Key phrases: Estaba cenando cuando sonó... / Era de noche / De repente / Mientras / Supe que.... Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column113: Unit 13.1: I can use lo as neuter object, answer yes-no questions with object pronouns, and use verbs of giving and telling.
column116: Goal: I can use lo as neuter object, answer yes-no questions with object pronouns, and use verbs of giving and telling. Key phrases: Lo sé / Lo parece / ¿Me lo das? / Le escribo / Le regalo. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column122: Unit 14.1: I can compare adjectives, adverbs, nouns and verbs with más, menos, tan and tanto, and use irregular comparatives.
column125: Goal: I can compare adjectives, adverbs, nouns and verbs with más, menos, tan and tanto, and use irregular comparatives. Key phrases: Más alto que / Tan grande como / Tanto como / Mejor / Mayor. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column131: Unit 15.1: I can contrast ser and estar fully, use estar with prepositions, contrast por and para, and use stressed possessives.
column134: Goal: I can contrast ser and estar fully, use estar with prepositions, contrast por and para, and use stressed possessives. Key phrases: Es aburrido / Está aburrido / Estoy de vacaciones / Para ti / Es mío. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column140: Unit 16.1: I can explain what the subjunctive is, recognize it in common phrases, and form regular and yo-stem present subjunctive.
column143: Goal: I can explain what the subjunctive is, recognize it in common phrases, and form regular and yo-stem present subjunctive. Key phrases: Quiero que hables / Es importante que comas / Ojalá que... / Que tengas suerte / Que hagas.... Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column149: Unit 17.1: I can express emotion, doubt and denial with the subjunctive using me alegro de que, dudo que and es raro que.
column152: Goal: I can express emotion, doubt and denial with the subjunctive using me alegro de que, dudo que and es raro que. Key phrases: Me alegro de que... / Siento que... / Dudo que... / No creo que... / Es raro que.... Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column158: Unit 18.1: I can use the five past tenses, irregular preterites, contrast preterite and imperfect, and revisit meaning-changing verbs.
column161: Goal: I can use the five past tenses, irregular preterites, contrast preterite and imperfect, and revisit meaning-changing verbs. Key phrases: Supe / Sabía / Conocí / Quería / Pude. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.
column167: Unit 19.1: I can choose between ir a and the future and form regular and irregular future tense verbs for plans and predictions.
column170: Goal: I can choose between ir a and the future and form regular and irregular future tense verbs for plans and predictions. Key phrases: Voy a viajar / Viajaré en mayo / Tendré tiempo / Saldremos pronto / Dirás la verdad. Hear them in a 30-second clip, repeat them, and guess their meaning before the lessons start.

column5: Welcome to Spanish: Where It Is Spoken and How It Sounds
column8: Meet Spanish in about 20 countries and across the US, and hear first words like hola, gracias, and amigo.
column14: Buenos Días, Buenas Tardes, Buenas Noches
column17: Greet people appropriately for the time of day and reply in kind, including the shortened Buen día and Buenas.
column26: Learn yo, tú, él, ella, nosotros, ellos and why Spanish usually omits them, so you say Soy Ana instead of Yo soy Ana.
column35: Conjugate hablar, trabajar, comprar, and estudiar with the six endings and use them without English subject pronouns.
column44: Conjugate estar and use it to say where people and things are, as in Estoy en casa and Los libros están aquí.
column53: Conjugate querer, pensar, empezar, and preferir where the stem changes in all forms except nosotros, using the boot pattern.
column62: Say what you like and dislike using me gusta and me gustan, and see why the thing liked is the grammatical subject.
column68: Reflexive Verbs Deep Dive: All Persons and Questions
column71: Revisit the reflexive pronouns me, te, se, nos, os, and se in questions and negatives, such as ¿Te levantas temprano? and No me acuesto tarde.
column77: Recognizing the Preterite: Yesterday, Last Night, Last Year
column80: Get input-first exposure to preterite forms in clear contexts and match them to finished-time markers before producing them.
column86: Preterite of Decir, Traer, and Conducir: J-Stems
column89: Form dije, trajeron, and condujeron, where the j-stem drops the i in the ustedes ending, and use them in reports.
column98: Form participles from known verbs, such as hablado, comido, and vivido, and recognize them in signs and labels.
column104: Completed vs Ongoing: The Core Rule of Thumb
column107: Learn the film-camera picture of the preterite as a snapshot and the imperfect as ongoing footage, with contrast pairs like Comí and Comía.
column113: Lo Soy, Lo Parece, No Lo Sé: Neuter Lo as Object
column116: Use neuter lo to replace adjectives, nouns after ser, and whole clauses, as in ¿Estás cansada? Sí, lo estoy and No lo sé.
column122: Comparing Adjectives and Adverbs: Más, Menos, Tan
column125: Build full comparisons with adjectives and adverbs, as in Ella es más alta que yo and Corre menos rápido que tú.
column131: Ser vs Estar Full Contrast: Aburrido, Listo, Malo, Rico
column134: Contrast ser and estar with adjectives that change meaning, such as es aburrido versus está aburrido and es listo versus está listo.
column140: What Is the Subjunctive? Mood vs Tense for English Speakers
column143: Understand mood as the speaker's stance, using English traces like I insist that he go, and see why Spanish uses it far more.
column149: Emotion Triggers: Me Alegro de Que, Siento Que, Me Molesta Que
column152: React to what others do with emotion verbs plus the subjunctive, as in Me alegro de que vengas.
column158: The Past Tense Map: Five Tenses and Their Jobs
column161: Draw a timeline that places the preterite, imperfect, present perfect, pluperfect, and progressive forms and states each tense's main job.
column167: Ir a versus the Future: Choosing Between Plans and Predictions
column170: Decide when to use voy a viajar for plans and viajaré for predictions, promises, and formal announcements in everyday Latin American speech.
column176: Direct versus Indirect Speech: The Big Picture
column179: Compare quoting words exactly, as in Dijo: Tengo hambre, with reporting them, as in Dijo que tenía hambre, and see what changes.
column185: Spotting the Imperfect Subjunctive: Recognition in Texts and Songs
column188: Recognize quisiera, tuviera, and hablara in short texts before producing them, learning what the -ra ending signals.
column194: B1 Self-Assessment: Can-Do Checklist and Personal Error Log
column197: Audit your skills against B1 can-do statements and start an error log of your recurring mistakes with examples.
column203: Emphatic Negation: Ni Siquiera, Nunca Jamás, Para Nada
column206: Strengthen negatives with ni siquiera, nunca jamás, para nada, and en absoluto, keeping double negatives such as No tengo nada correct, unlike English.
column212: Stating an Opinion: Creo Que, Pienso Que, Me Parece Que
column215: Give opinions clearly with indicative after affirmative verbs, as in Creo que tienes razón and Me parece que es injusto.
column221: Cohesion: What Makes a Text Hold Together
column224: Identify how connectors, pronouns, repetition, and structure link sentences and ideas in short Spanish texts.
column230: The Media Landscape: Prensa, Radio, Televisión, and Digital
column233: Name the main kinds of media and outlets in the Spanish-speaking world and say how you get your news, as in leo el periódico digital.
column239: Anatomy of a Complex Sentence: Main Clause, Subordinate Clause, Embedding
column242: Identify main and subordinate clauses in long Spanish sentences, mark noun, adjective, and adverbial clauses, and see how they nest.
column248: Passive with Ser: Forming La Casa Fue Construida
column251: Build ser plus participle with agreement, as in La carta fue escrita, Los libros son leídos, and Las puertas serán abiertas.
column257: Pluperfect Subjunctive: Forming Hubiera plus Participle
column260: Build hubiera hablado, hubieras comido, and hubieran vuelto from the imperfect subjunctive of haber plus the participle, including irregular participles.
column266: The Register Spectrum: Formal, Neutral, Colloquial, and Vulgar
column269: Place words and sentences along a scale of formality and choose the right level for a boss, a friend, or a public speech.
column275: B2 Self-Assessment: Can-Do Checklist and Personal Error Log
column278: Rate your abilities against B2 descriptors, collect your recurring errors, and set a plan for filling gaps.
column284: What Makes Spanish Academic: Register and Conventions
column287: Recognize the traits of academic Spanish such as impersonal voice, dense noun phrases, and precise verbs, and compare short academic and everyday passages.
column293: The Art of Persuasion: Logos, Ethos, and Pathos
column296: Analyze how a Spanish speaker persuades through logic, credibility, and emotion, using short political and advertising texts as examples.
column302: Dinner-Table Listening: Following Four Speakers Who Overlap
column305: Track who says what when friends talk over each other, using names, voices, and reactions like ¡no, espérate! as anchors.
column311: Professional Register and Workplace Communication in Spanish
column314: Adjust tone, formality, and structure across workplaces, using courtesy formulas such as le agradecería and quedo a su disposición.
column320: C1 Self-Assessment: Can-Do Map and Personal Error Log
column323: Map your abilities against C1 descriptors, build an error log from recent recordings and essays, and set targets such as fewer dequeísmo slips.
column329: Small Talk Like a Local: Weather, Traffic, Family, and Food
column332: Open and sustain light conversation with natural openers like ¡Qué calor!, ¿Y la familia?, and ¿Cómo estuvo el tráfico?
column338: How Meaning Exceeds Words: Pragmatics and Nuance in Spanish
column341: Learn why the same sentence, such as qué bien, can praise or complain, and how context and tone decide meaning.
column347: Dialect Ear Diagnostic: Placing a Speaker in 30 Seconds
column350: Identify likely origin from short clips by noticing consonant weakening, vowel behavior, intonation, and telltale words.
column356: Disputing a Wrong Charge with a Bank or Phone Company
column359: Challenge an incorrect bill by phone and chat with me aparece un cargo que no reconozco and quiero levantar una aclaración.
column365: Classical Rhetoric: Inventio, Dispositio, Elocutio, Memoria, and Actio
column368: Apply the five canons of rhetoric to plan a Spanish speech, using terms such as exordio, narración, argumentación, and peroración.
column374: Defining Distinguished Spanish: ACTFL Distinguished and ILR 4 to 5
column377: Study the descriptors of Distinguished and ILR 5 performance, self-assess against them, and build a plan for the remaining gaps in each skill.
column383: Studying History and Culture in Spanish: Sources and Method
column386: Read historical narratives, primary sources, and timelines in Spanish, using terms like fuente primaria, periodización, and historiografía to take structured notes.
column392: Chicano Movement, Farmworkers, and Young Lords
column395: Study Chávez and Huerta, the Chicano student walkouts, the Young Lords, and movement slogans and posters, reading manifestos such as El Plan de Aztlán.
column401: How to Read Literature in Spanish: Strategies and Glossaries
column404: Prepare to read literary texts with context research, annotated editions, and reading logs, and learn to tolerate unknown words in poetry and prose.
column410: Garcilaso II: Sonetos I, V, and XIII and Petrarchism
column413: Compare sonnets of love, suffering, and myth and identify Petrarchan conventions in Spanish.
column419: Timeline of Spanish Literature from the Enlightenment to the Present
column422: Place movements from Neoclassicism to the postwar novel on a timeline, and see how history shaped each literary reaction.
column428: Lorca I: Romancero gitano and Romance sonámbulo
column431: Read the ballad with commentary, analyze its images of green and night, and note the modern use of the romance form.
column437: Colonial Latin America: Voices of Conquest and Resistance
column440: Learn the historical frame of conquest and colony and how chroniclers, indigenous writers, and mestizos told competing versions of events.
column446: Rulfo's No oyes ladrar los perros and Rural Violence
column449: Read the story of a father carrying his wounded son, and analyze dialogue, silence, and the harsh landscape of Jalisco.
column455: Translation, Adaptation, and Mediation: Mapping the Field
column458: Distinguish translation, interpreting, localization, transcreation, and mediation, and see how each shapes decisions about faithfulness.
column464: Interpreting Modes, Settings, and the Profession
column467: Distinguish consecutive, simultaneous, whispered, sight, and remote interpreting, and map settings from clinics to courts to conferences.
column473: What Is Linguistics? Levels of Analysis and Descriptive versus Prescriptive Grammar
column476: Learn the core fields of linguistics and their Spanish terms, and separate describing usage from prescribing rules.
column485: Frame why Spanish varies by region, class, age, and situation, and learn core terms such as variable, variante, norma, and comunidad de habla.
column494: Trace semantic shift such as broadening, narrowing, and metaphor, and etymologies of Arabic loans like aceite and ojalá, using Corominas.
column500: Becoming a Spanish Teacher: Roles, Ethics, and Professional Identity
column503: Reflect on what teaching Spanish demands, from expertise to cultural humility, and learn how to describe your qualifications and philosophy in Spanish.
column509: Entering Hispanic Studies: Fields, Journals, and Conversations
column512: Map the subfields of literature, linguistics, cultural studies, and pedagogy, and identify major journals such as Hispania, Hispanic Review, and MLN.

column8: Recognize hundreds of Spanish words you already understand from English, such as hotel, restaurante, familia, importante, and música, and learn how to spot them.

column23: Ser Present Singular: Soy, Eres, Es

column35: Conjugate comer, beber, aprender, and leer, and see how -er endings differ from -ar in the tú, nosotros, and ellos forms.
column44: Say how people feel or what state things are in with estoy cansado, está abierto, and están contentos, and agree the adjective.
column53: Conjugate poder, dormir, volver, and encontrar, and add jugar with u to ue, using the same boot pattern.
column62: Talk about activities you enjoy with gustar plus a verb, such as Me gusta bailar and No me gusta cocinar.
column68: Reflexive Pronoun Placement with Infinitives and Gerunds
column71: Attach or place pronouns correctly, saying both Voy a levantarme and Me voy a levantar, and Estoy duchándome or Me estoy duchando.
column80: Form and use hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, and hablaron to say what you did, such as Ayer trabajé mucho.
column89: Use the third-person change in pidió, durmió, murió, and sintieron, while nosotros and tú forms stay regular.
column98: Memorize the frequent irregulars hecho, dicho, visto, escrito, puesto, vuelto, abierto, roto, and muerto through short chunks.
column104: Interrupted Actions: Estaba Cenando Cuando Sonó el Teléfono
column107: Combine imperfect or imperfect progressive with a preterite interruption, as in Dormía cuando llamaste.
column113: Answering Yes-No Questions with Object Pronouns
column116: Practice quick pronoun answers such as ¿Compraste el pan? Sí, lo compré, and No, no lo compré, in real exchanges.
column122: Comparing Nouns and Verbs: Más Que, Más De, Tanto Como
column125: Compare quantities and actions, and use de before numbers, as in Tengo más de tres primos and Trabajo tanto como tú.
column131: Estar De, En, Con, Para, and Por: Estar de Vacaciones
column134: Use estar with prepositions in set phrases, such as estar de vacaciones, en huelga, con gripe, para salir, and por hacer.
column140: Recognizing the Subjunctive in Everyday Phrases
column143: Notice subjunctive forms already heard in chunks like Que tengas un buen día, Que aproveche, and Ojalá que sí.
column152: Learn 15 verbs and phrases of feeling, such as temer, sorprender, lamentar, and me da pena, and sort them by pattern.
column158: Irregular Preterites Retrieval: Families, Stems, and Spelling
column161: Test recall of all irregular preterite families and spelling changes through timed sorting and short story gaps.
column167: Regular Future Forms Rebuilt on the Infinitive
column170: Add the endings -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -án to the whole infinitive, as in hablaré, comerás, and viviremos.
column176: Reporting Verbs: Decir, Contar, Explicar, Preguntar, Responder
column179: Choose the right verb to introduce what people said, as in Me explicó que and Le respondí que no.
column185: Forming the Imperfect Subjunctive: The Ellos Preterite Stem
column188: Drop -ron from the third-person plural preterite and add -ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran, as in hablaron to hablara.
column194: Vosotros in the Present and Commands
column197: Produce Spain-style forms like habláis, coméis, and venid, and know when vosotros is expected.
column203: Ya as a Discourse Particle: Ya Sé, Ya Veremos, Ya Mismo
column206: Read the many meanings of ya beyond already, as in Ya sé, Ya veremos, Ya mismo, and Ya no, and distinguish aún and todavía.
column212: Negated Opinion in Formal Registers: No Considero Que
column215: Use the subjunctive after negated opinion verbs in formal talk, as in No considero que sea justo and No estoy convencido de que sea posible.
column221: Connectors of Addition: Además, Asimismo, Incluso, Tampoco
column224: Add ideas using además, asimismo, encima, incluso, and tampoco, and place them naturally in a sentence.
column230: The Newspaper: Sections and Front Page Vocabulary
column233: Navigate secciones such as Internacional, Sociedad, Economía, and Cultura, and use portada, titular, and columna to talk about a newspaper.
column239: Subject-Verb Agreement Puzzles: La Mayoría, Uno de los Que, Juan y Yo
column242: Settle hard agreements such as la mayoría de los estudiantes, uno de los que, Juan y yo, and la causa fueron las lluvias.
column248: The Agent: Por versus De and Leaving the Agent Out
column251: Add the doer with por, use de after feelings or states like respetado de todos, and learn when Spanish omits the agent entirely.
column257: The Hubiese Form and Regional Preferences
column260: Recognize hubiese hablado as an equal variant of hubiera hablado, and see where each form is preferred in writing and speech.
column266: Pitch and Pace by Register: Formal versus Casual Speech
column269: Shift speed, pitch range, and articulation between a formal talk and a casual chat, as in Buenas tardes, señores versus ¿Qué onda?
column275: Retrieval Review: The Whole Tense and Mood System on One Page
column278: Recall every indicative, subjunctive, and conditional tense by form and use, and fill a full map from memory.
column284: Reading Strategies: Previewing, Skimming, and Scanning
column287: Preview titles, abstracts, and topic sentences to predict content, then skim for gist and scan for data in unfamiliar Spanish articles.
column296: Adapt tone, examples, and vocabulary to the audience and situation, comparing a message to students, voters, and executives.
column302: Understanding Audios: WhatsApp Voice Notes from Friends and Family
column305: Follow rambling voice notes with background noise, restarts, and asides, such as Oye, este, nada, que te quería decir que.
column314: Learn vocabulary for the cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, and nervous systems, such as corazón, pulmones, and riñones, and how to describe pain.
column320: Retrieval Review: Verb Morphology and Irregular Forms at Speed
column323: Retrieve every tense and mood quickly, including rare irregulars such as satisfice, hubiere, and cupieran, through timed drills and cloze texts.
column329: Greeting a Whole Room: Saludar a Todos and Group Etiquette
column332: Greet and kiss or shake hands with everyone at a gathering, and understand why skipping someone reads as rude.
column338: Implicature and Reading Between the Lines
column341: Infer what speakers imply but do not say, using Grice's maxims with examples like no está mal and podrías cerrar la ventana.
column347: Building a Dialect Profile: Sounds, Grammar, Lexicon, and Pragmatics
column350: Use a four-part template to describe any variety systematically and compare it with your base variety.
column356: Talking Money in Plain Words: Loans, Credit, Debts, and Mortgages
column359: Discuss personal finances naturally, using pedir un préstamo, historial crediticio, estar endeudado, and la hipoteca, with friends and advisers.
column365: Ethos, Pathos, and Logos in Spanish Persuasion
column368: Analyze how speakers build credibility, emotion, and reasoning in Spanish, and identify each appeal in a short political or advertising text.
column374: Self-Audit: Mapping Your Spanish Across All Skills and Domains
column377: Use a profile grid to rate reading, listening, speaking, writing, mediation, and cultural knowledge, and select targets for capstone work.
column383: Pre-Columbian Civilizations: Maya, Mexica, Inca, and Taíno
column386: Describe the political, religious, and agricultural systems of major Americas civilizations and learn key terms such as calendario, tributo, and cacicazgo.
column392: Chicano Movement Deeper: Tijerina, Corky Gonzales, Teatro Campesino, and Chicana Feminism
column395: Study land-grant activism, Yo Soy Joaquín, El Teatro Campesino, and Chicana feminist writers, reading excerpts in Spanish and English.
column401: Literary Terms I: Narrador, Trama, Personaje, Tema, and Símbolo
column404: Learn ten core terms of literary analysis such as narrador, trama, símbolo, and ambiente, and apply them to a short story.
column410: Boscán, Herrera, and the Italianate Turn in Spanish Verse
column413: Trace how the eleven-syllable line and sonnet arrived from Italy through Boscán and how Herrera and the Sevillian school refined them.
column419: Enlightenment and Neoclassicism: Feijoo, Jovellanos, and Moratín
column422: Read excerpts, including El sí de las niñas, and see how reason, reform, and moral teaching shaped 18th century writing.
column428: Lorca II: Poeta en Nueva York
column431: Read poems from the New York period and discuss urban alienation, race, and surreal imagery.
column437: Columbus's Letters and Diario: First Encounters
column440: Read the Carta a Luis de Santángel and log entries to see how Columbus's descriptions shaped European fantasies of the New World.
column449: Read the novel of a ghost town, following its fragmented voices, time shifts, and death as a setting.
column455: Translation Brief, Skopos, and Text-Type Analysis
column458: Read a commission for purpose, audience, and function, and classify a source as informative, expressive, or operative before translating.
column467: Trace Nuremberg, the Geneva school, and community interpreting research, and connect Gile's Effort Models to practice.
column473: Articulatory Phonetics I: Vocal Tract and Airstream
column476: Name the organs of speech and describe how airflow and voicing produce sounds, using Spanish terminology.
column485: Read how researchers elicit vernacular speech through the sociolinguistic interview, observer's paradox, and reading-style tasks, and plan a short Spanish interview module.
column491: Historical Corpora: CORDE, CDH, and Corpus del Nuevo Mundo
column494: Search diachronic corpora to date a construction or word, set search filters, and read frequency curves and examples critically.
column503: Use an observation protocol to record teacher talk, student output, and method, and give respectful feedback such as me llamó la atención que.
column509: Reading Scholarship in Spanish: Strategies for Academic Prose
column512: Read dense articles efficiently by finding thesis, method, and evidence, and take notes with phrases like el autor sostiene and a mi juicio.

column5: Hola, Adiós, and Your First Greetings
column8: Recognize and echo the very first greeting words hola, adiós, buenos días, and hasta luego, before Level 2 builds full greetings.
column14: How Are You: Cómo Estás and Answering
column17: Ask and answer how someone is, using bien, mal, más o menos, muy bien, and ¿Y tú?
column26: Complete the present of ser with somos and son for plural subjects, as in Somos amigos and Ellas son de Chile.
column35: Conjugate vivir, escribir, abrir, and recibir, and notice where -ir matches -er and where it differs.
column41: Ser vs Estar: Choosing Between Them
column44: Decide between ser for identity, origin, and traits and estar for location and state using clear cases like Es alto and Está en casa.
column53: Conjugate pedir, servir, repetir, and seguir, and separate them from e to ie verbs such as sentir.
column59: A mí me gusta: Emphasis and Other People
column62: Ask and answer about other people's tastes with te, le, nos, and les, plus emphasis like A ti te gusta and A ella le gusta.
column68: Direct Object Pronoun Placement with Infinitives and Gerunds
column71: Place the pronoun before the conjugated verb or attach it to the end, as in Lo quiero comprar and Estoy comprándolo.
column80: Form comí, comiste, comió, viví, and vivieron, and notice the shared endings and that -ir nosotros matches the present.
column86: Preterite of Leer, Oír, Caer, Creer, and Construir
column89: Write leyó, oyeron, cayó, creyó, and construyó, where i between vowels becomes y and other forms take an accent.
column98: Build the perfect with he, has, ha, hemos, and han, as in He comido and Hemos terminado, and compare with English have.
column104: Setting the Scene, Then the Plot
column107: Structure a story with imperfect background followed by preterite events, as in Era de noche y llovía; entonces oí un ruido.
column113: Usted and Ustedes with Lo, La, Le, and Se
column116: Choose the right object pronoun for formal you, as in La vi a usted and Se lo explico a ustedes.
column122: Irregular Comparatives: Mejor, Peor, Mayor, Menor
column125: Use mejor, peor, mayor, and menor instead of más bueno or más viejo, as in Mi hermana mayor cocina mejor.
column134: Sort por and para by function in mixed sentences, such as Trabajo para una empresa, Gracias por todo, and Salgo para Lima.
column140: Regular Present Subjunctive: Switching the Vowel
column143: Form the present subjunctive by swapping -a and -e endings, as in hable, coma, and viva, and drill every person.
column149: Impersonal Emotion Expressions: Es Bueno Que, Es Triste Que, Es Raro Que
column152: Comment on situations with impersonal expressions, as in Es increíble que ganemos and Es una lástima que llueva.
column158: Preterite vs Imperfect Full Contrast: Boundaries and Beginnings
column161: Decide between the two tenses at a deeper level using completed, ongoing, habitual, and background cues, with side-by-side pairs.
column167: Future Stems Rebuilt I: Tener, Poner, Salir, Venir, Valer
column170: Retrieve the d-stems tendr-, pondr-, saldr-, vendr-, and valdr- in longer sentences and short paragraphs, as in Mañana saldré temprano y vendré tarde.
column176: Vocabulary: Speech Verbs and Communication Acts
column179: Learn 15 frequent verbs like afirmar, sugerir, admitir, negar, aclarar, and añadir, with the constructions they take.
column185: Regular -ar Verbs in the Imperfect Subjunctive
column188: Practice hablara, cantaras, trabajáramos, and estudiaran in short sentences with quería que.
column194: Vosotros in the Future and Subjunctive: Hablaréis, Queráis
column197: Extend vosotros to hablaréis, queráis, and viajaríais, review hablasteis, and compare each with the ustedes forms of Latin America.
column203: Emphatic Yes: Sí Que, Claro Que Sí, Ya Lo Creo, Vaya Si
column206: Strengthen a yes with sí que, claro que sí, por supuesto, ya lo creo, and vaya si, choosing the right intensity.
column212: Stance Phrases: En Mi Opinión, Desde Mi Punto de Vista, Para Mí
column215: Frame a viewpoint with a range of introductory phrases suited to conversation and writing.
column221: Ordering and Digressing: En Primer Lugar, Por Cierto, A Propósito, Dicho Esto
column224: Structure talk and writing with en primer lugar, por otra parte, and en último término, and drift off-topic with por cierto.
column230: Reading Headlines: Titulares and Their Shortcuts
column233: Decode headline grammar such as the present tense for past events, dropped articles, and noun strings, as in Aprueban una ley de migración.
column239: Noun Clauses: Que, Si, and Question Words as Subjects and Objects
column242: Build sentences like Depende de si llueve, No sé cuándo llegan, and Me preocupa que no responda, and choose the right conjunction.
column248: Passive in Every Tense: Fue Aprobado, Ha Sido Publicado, Será Entregado
column251: Use the ser passive in the preterite, present perfect, and future, and recognize it in news and formal writing.
column260: Form habría dicho, habrías podido, and habrían ido, and use them for what would have happened, as in Yo habría ayudado.
column266: Register Pairs: Comprar and Adquirir, Empezar and Comenzar
column269: Learn formal and informal equivalents such as dinero and capital, ayudar and colaborar, and irse and marcharse, and choose by situation.
column275: Spiral Review: Subjunctive Triggers Across All Tenses in One Text
column278: Read a long text and explain each subjunctive choice, from present perfect to pluperfect, with volition, emotion, doubt, and condition.
column284: Finding the Thesis and Mapping an Argument
column287: Locate the tesis, supporting premises, and conclusion of a Spanish essay, and sketch its structure as an outline in your own words.
column293: The Five Canons of Rhetoric: Inventio to Actio
column296: Get a first map of inventio, dispositio, elocutio, memoria, and actio and see each at work in a famous Spanish-language speech.
column302: Watching Series Without Subtitles: A Graduated Plan
column305: Move from Spanish subtitles to none using rewatching, scene summaries, and a weekly target of unsubtitled minutes in Spanish-language series.
column314: Master terms such as diabetes, hipertensión, asma, infección, and cáncer, and talk about chronic illness and prevention.
column320: Rare Literary Tenses: Hubiere Hablado and Hubo Hablado
column323: Read the future subjunctive and pretérito anterior in laws, proverbs, and older prose, as in Si hubiere lugar and Apenas hubo salido.
column329: The Long Goodbye: Leave-Taking Rituals and Ya Me Voy
column332: Manage the slow exit natives expect, from bueno, ya me voy to the final goodbyes at the door twenty minutes later.
column338: Register Shifting on Demand: One Message in Five Registers
column341: Rewrite a request from slang to legal prose, adjusting vocabulary, syntax, and address forms to fit each audience.
column350: Recognize aspiration of s, lenition of d, velarized n, assibilated r, and lateral r, and hear them in real speech.
column356: Explaining Trámites Casually: Paperwork Stories Among Friends
column359: Tell and follow everyday stories about bureaucracy, such as me mandaron de ventanilla en ventanilla and me faltó una copia.
column365: Rhetorical Figures in Oratory: Anáfora, Antítesis, Gradación, and Clímax
column368: Recognize and use figures of repetition and contrast that structure Spanish speeches, such as anáfora and tricolon, in analysis and in your own drafts.
column374: Reading at Distinguished Level I: Dense Prose and Implicit Argument
column377: Read essays and editorials that rely on allusion, irony, and long sentences, and paraphrase both explicit and implicit claims.
column383: Prehistoric and Pre-Roman Iberia: Altamira, Iberians, Celts, and Phoenician Colonies
column386: Trace Iberia from Atapuerca and Altamira through Iberians, Celtiberians, Tartessos, and Phoenician, Greek, and Carthaginian colonies to Rome.
column392: Latino Civil Rights Cases: Mendez, Hernandez v Texas, LULAC, and MALDEF
column395: Explain landmark school and jury cases and the organizations that brought them, using legal vocabulary such as demanda and segregación.
column401: Literary Terms II: Point of View, Time, and Structure
column404: Describe narrative voice, focalization, flashbacks, and framing with terms like narrador omnisciente, in medias res, and relato enmarcado.
column410: Erasmism and Humanist Dialogue: Alfonso de Valdés and Sixteenth-Century Prose
column413: Read humanist prose in dialogue form and see how Erasmian criticism of the Church shaped Spanish writing before the Inquisition tightened.
column419: Cadalso's Cartas marruecas and Enlightenment Satire
column422: Read letters from an invented Moroccan visitor who criticizes Spanish customs, and see how epistolary satire questions the nation.
column428: Lorca: Llanto por Ignacio Sánchez Mejías and Sonetos del amor oscuro
column431: Read the elegy for the bullfighter and Lorca's late love sonnets, and analyze repetition, refrain, and sacred and erotic imagery.
column440: Read excerpts of the shipwreck and eight-year journey across North America, and analyze the first-person account of transformation.
column446: Alejo Carpentier: Lo real maravilloso and Viaje a la semilla
column449: Read the prologue and story and discuss the marvelous real in Caribbean history and time reversal.
column455: Reading as a Translator: Analyzing a Source Text
column458: Annotate register, tone, terminology, cohesion devices, and difficulties before drafting, using a repeatable checklist.
column464: Cognitive Skills of Interpreting: Listening, Memory, and Multitasking
column467: Diagnose your baseline and learn how listening, analysis, memory, and production compete in real-time work.
column473: Articulatory Phonetics II: Places and Manners of Consonants
column476: Classify Spanish consonants by place, manner, and voicing, such as oclusiva bilabial sorda for p.
column482: Variationist Analysis: Variables, Variants, and Constraints
column485: Define a linguistic variable, its variants, and the envelope of variation, and read tables of factor weights for a variable like -s deletion.
column491: Spanish in the Americas: Koineization and the Andalusian Hypothesis
column494: Weigh explanations for American Spanish features, including settlement patterns, koine formation, the tierras altas and bajas model, and indigenous substrate claims.
column500: ACTFL World-Readiness Standards and the Five Cs
column503: Use Communication, Cultures, Connections, Comparisons, and Communities to frame goals, and write unit objectives that address each standard.
column509: Formulating a Research Question and Argument
column512: Turn a topic into a defensible research question, a claim, and a gap statement, and test it against counterarguments.

column5: The Five Pure Vowels A E I O U
column8: Pronounce Spanish vowels as short, clear, steady sounds in words like casa, mesa, mini, foto, and uno.
column17: Leave a conversation politely with adiós, hasta luego, hasta mañana, nos vemos, and chao, matching the moment.
column26: Understand why Latin America says ustedes for all plural you while Spain distinguishes vosotros, and hear both in short clips.
column35: Conjugate the irregular verb ir and use it with adónde to say where people are going, as in Voy al trabajo.
column41: Ser for Events, Time, Material, and Origin
column44: Use ser for where an event takes place, time, material, and origin, as in La fiesta es en mi casa and Es de madera.
column53: Mix all three stem-change patterns in short conversations to build automatic use of quiero, puedo, pido, and duermo.
column59: Encantar, Odiar, and Degrees of Liking
column62: Express strong feelings and shades of preference with me encanta, odio, prefiero, and no me gusta nada, for example Me encanta el chocolate.
column68: Wishes as Chunks: Ojalá, Espero Que, Quiero Que
column71: Recognize and use ojalá and quiero que as memorized chunks in greetings and wishes, before studying the subjunctive itself.
column77: Accent Marks and Endings: Hablo vs Habló
column80: Hear and write the difference between present and preterite, such as compro and compró, and stress the final syllable.
column86: Meaning Changes in the Preterite: Saber, Conocer, Querer, Poder
column89: First look at how supe means found out, conocí means met, quise means tried, and no pude means failed.
column98: Form ¿Has visto...? and No he terminado, keeping haber and the participle together with pronouns before haber and no do-support.
column107: Master conocer, saber, querer, poder, and tener in both tenses, such as Sabía que... versus Supe que... in stories.
column113: Verbs of Giving and Telling: Dar, Decir, Escribir, Mandar, Regalar
column116: Use high-frequency transfer verbs with indirect objects, such as Me dijo la verdad, Les mandé un mensaje, and Te regalo esto.
column122: Equality: Tan Como, Tanto Como, and Igual Que
column125: Say two things are equal with tan...como, tanto/a/os/as...como, and igual de, matching gender and number correctly.
column131: Stressed Possessives: Mío, Tuyo, Suyo, Nuestro
column134: Use el mío, la tuya, and de nosotros for ownership, as in ¿Es tuyo este libro? No, es mío.
column140: Yo-Form Stems: Tener, Hacer, Salir, Conocer, Decir
column143: Build subjunctive stems from the yo form of irregular verbs, as in tenga, haga, salga, conozca, and diga.
column149: Doubt and Denial: No Creo Que, Dudo Que, No Es Verdad Que
column152: Express uncertainty with the subjunctive, as in Dudo que sea cierto and No creo que tengas razón.
column158: Mental States and Meaning-Changing Verbs Revisited
column161: Add negation and duration to Supe and Sabía, Conocí and Conocía, and No quise versus No quería, as in No pude abrirla and Podía nadar.
column167: Future Stems Rebuilt II: Decir, Hacer, Haber, Poder, Querer, Saber
column170: Retrieve the shortened stems dir-, har-, habr-, podr-, querr-, and sabr- at speed in connected sentences like Haré lo que pueda y te diré.
column176: Reporting Statements in the Present: Dice que
column179: Relay what someone says right now with no tense change, as in Mi jefe dice que la reunión es a las tres.
column185: Regular -er and -ir Verbs in the Imperfect Subjunctive
column188: Practice comiera, vivieras, escribiéramos, and salieran, and see that -er and -ir share endings.
column194: Voseo in Commands and Questions: Vení, Decime, Vos Querés
column197: Extend voseo recognition to commands and questions such as Vení, Decime, and Vos querés in Argentine, Uruguayan, and Central American audio, without producing them yet.
column203: Emphatic Yes: Sí Que, Claro Que Sí, Ya Lo Creo
column206: Strengthen agreement with sí que, claro que sí, por supuesto, ya lo creo, and vaya si, and choose a level suited to the setting.
column212: Advanced Hedges: Más Bien, Digamos, and En Cierto Modo
column215: Soften claims with más bien, digamos, en cierto modo, and me da la impresión de que, beyond the basic hedges already learned.
column221: Focus Words: Solo, Incluso, Hasta, Ni Siquiera, Tan Siquiera
column224: Use focus adverbs to highlight one element, contrasting solo, incluso, hasta, and siquiera in sentences like Hasta él lo sabía.
column230: Anatomy of a News Story: Entradilla, Cuerpo, and Cierre
column233: Find who, what, when, where, and why in the lead and body of a report, using entradilla and cuerpo.
column239: Uses of Que: Conjunction, Comparison, Exhortative, and Repeated Que
column242: Sort the many jobs of que, including the conjunction, comparative, exhortative, and repeated que in Te dije que, si vienes, que te avise.
column248: Passive with Modals and Infinitives: Debe Ser Resuelto, Puede Ser Visto
column251: Combine the passive with modal verbs and infinitives to say what must, can, or should be done in reports and rules.
column257: Si-Clauses Type Three: Si Hubiera Sabido, Habría Venido

column5: Sí, No, Por Favor, Gracias, De Nada
column8: Use the five most useful polite survival words in short exchanges and respond naturally.
column14: My Name Is: Me Llamo and Cómo Te Llamas
column17: Say your name and ask someone else's with me llamo, ¿cómo te llamas?, and mi nombre es.
column26: Assign masculine and feminine to most nouns by their endings, as in el libro, la casa, el amigo, and la amiga.
column32: Querer, Poder, and Preferir with Infinitives
column35: Combine conjugated modal verbs with infinitives to express wants and ability, as in Quiero comer and No puedo salir.
column41: The Preposition De: Modifiers, Cause, and Partitives
column44: Use de in una caja de madera, un vaso de agua, morir de frío, and algo de comer to link nouns and express cause.
column50: Fluency Drill: Fast Answers with Quiero, Puedo, Tengo Que, and Voy a
column53: Answer rapid prompts with the four most useful verb frames plus infinitive until each response comes without translating.
column59: Agreeing and Disagreeing: También, Tampoco, Yo sí, Yo no
column62: React to opinions about likes with A mí también, A mí tampoco, Yo sí, and Yo no, avoiding the English "me neither" trap.
column68: Meaning-Changing Pairs: Ir and Irse, Dormir and Dormirse
column71: Contrast ir with irse, dormir with dormirse, and llamar with llamarse to see how a reflexive changes meaning, as in Me voy and Me duermo.
column77: Hace plus Time: How Long Ago
column80: Say how long ago something happened using hace tres años, and contrast the English ago.
column86: Preterite Complete Review: Sorting the Irregular Families
column89: Use retrieval practice to sort every preterite pattern learned so far and produce forms rapidly in short prompts.
column95: No, Nunca, Ya, and Pronouns Around Haber
column98: Place negatives, adverbs, and clitics with compound tenses, as in No lo he visto nunca and Ya se lo he dicho.
column104: Ser, Estar, and Haber in Past Narration
column107: Choose among era, fue, estaba, estuvo, había, and hubo when narrating scenes and events.
column113: Direct or Indirect Object? Ayudar, Llamar, Preguntar, Pegar, Escuchar
column116: Decide which verbs take lo or le, as in Lo ayudé, Le pregunté, Lo llamé, Le pegó, and avoid English-based guesses.
column122: Too and Enough: Demasiado Para, Lo Bastante Para, Tan Como Para
column125: Say too much and enough with demasiado para, lo bastante para, and tan ... como para, as in Es demasiado tarde para llamar.
column131: Clarifying Su: De Él, De Ella, De Ustedes
column134: Avoid ambiguity with su by adding de él, de ella, or de ustedes, and choose between su casa and la casa de ella.

column5: Vowel Discipline: No Schwa, No Glide
column8: Stop the English habit of reducing and gliding vowels so that words like todo, banana, and momento keep every vowel crisp.
column14: Nice to Meet You: Mucho Gusto and Encantado
column17: Respond when meeting someone, with mucho gusto, encantado or encantada, igualmente, and el gusto es mío.
column26: Form plurals with -s and -es, including the z to c change, in libros, lápices, and canciones.
column35: Tell the hour with Es la una and Son las tres, and ask ¿Qué hora es?
column41: Hay: There Is and There Are
column44: Use hay with articles and quantities, as in Hay un parque, No hay leche, and ¿Hay un banco por aquí?
column50: Yo-Irregular Verbs: Ver, Dar, Saber, Conducir
column53: Learn veo, doy, sé, and conduzco, and use them in everyday sentences about what you do and know.
column59: High-Frequency Nouns and Adjectives for A1 Fluency
column62: Consolidate the most frequent nouns and adjectives, such as cosa, persona, tiempo, bueno, grande, and mismo, in simple sentences.
column68: Linking Routine Actions with Mientras and Cuando
column71: Link routine actions with mientras, cuando, and después de plus infinitive, building on primero and luego, as in Mientras me ducho, escucho música.
column77: Negatives and Questions in the Preterite
column80: Ask ¿Comiste?, ¿Qué hiciste?, and answer No comí, without English did as a helping verb.
column86: Desde, Hasta, Hacia, A Partir De, and A Través De
column89: Use desde, hasta, hacia, a partir de, and a través de for time and space, as in a partir de mañana.
column95: Perfect with Reflexives and Pronoun Chunks
column98: Place pronouns before haber in Me he levantado, Nos hemos visto, and Lo he hecho, avoiding attachment to the participle.
column107: Use A los diez años versus Tenía diez años, and Eran las tres versus A las tres, in stories.
column113: Gustar-Type Verbs: Interesar, Importar, Molestar, Fascinar
column116: Extend the gustar pattern to feelings and reactions, such as Me interesa la música and Nos molestan los ruidos.
column122: Superlatives: El Más, La Menos, Los Mejores
column125: Say the most or least in a group with de, as in Es el restaurante más caro de la ciudad.
column131: Indefinite and Negative Words: Alguien, Algo, Alguno, Ninguno, Cada
column134: Use alguien, nadie, algo, nada, algún, ningún, and cada, including double negatives like No veo a nadie.

column296: Build and test arguments using the syllogism and generalization from cases, with phrases like de ahí se deduce que and por tanto.

column242: Combine a present main clause with a past subordinate action, as in Me alegra que ayer vinieras, and learn when the rule bends.

column251: Rewrite a passive sentence three ways, such as Construyeron el puente, Se construyó el puente, and Un equipo construyó el puente.

column269: Use momentito, cafecito, and ahorita to add warmth or soften requests, and know when a diminutive changes meaning.

column314: Explain vacunación, tamizaje, and Lávese las manos, and design clear campaign messages for community audiences.

column323: Master lexicalized uses such as por si acaso, para colmo, no estar para bromas, and por lo que se ve.

column332: Respond to praise the native way with ay, qué va, ¿tú crees?, es viejo, or gracias, tú también.

column341: Express and detect unexpected information and speaker attitude with intensifying and exclamatory constructions.
column347: Voseo III: Central America and Its Mixed Systems
column350: Compare voseo in Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Costa Rica, including tuteo, ustedeo, and social conditioning.

column368: Use Spanish intonation patterns, pauses, and focus to control meaning, and record yourself giving a two-minute talk for feedback.

column377: Understand and appropriately use slang from Mexico, Spain, Argentina, Colombia, Chile, and the Caribbean, including taboo words and their social force.

column386: Follow the Acapulco-Manila trade route, silver, silk, and the cultural exchanges that connected Mexico, the Philippines, and China.
column392: Latinx Studies: Identity, Panethnicity, and Census Categories
column395: Discuss Hispanic, Latino, Latina, Latinx, and Latine, census categories, and identity debates using scholarly and community writing.
column401: Cuaderna Vía, Pie Quebrado, Cesura, and Hemistiquio
column404: Analyze long lines split at the cesura, Berceo's fourteen-syllable stanzas, and Manrique's short pie quebrado, marking half-lines such as Recuerde el alma dormida.
column410: Lazarillo de Tormes II: Tratado I and the Blind Master
column413: Read the original text of the first tratado, tracing how Lázaro learns to survive and lose innocence.
column422: Read one legend, such as Los ojos verdes or El monte de las ánimas, and analyze atmosphere and narrative devices.
column428: Lorca V: La casa de Bernarda Alba, Acts II and III
column431: Follow the escalating conflict and analyze the play's ending and its political and social readings.
column437: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega: Comentarios reales and the Mestizo Voice
column440: Read passages that present Inca history and language from a mestizo perspective.
column446: García Márquez Stories: La siesta del martes, El ahogado más hermoso
column449: Read two short stories and analyze small-town silence, mother love, and how a drowned stranger transforms a village.

column458: Study Nida and Newmark on formal versus dynamic equivalence, then apply their contrasting positions to short texts and defend a choice.

column467: Interpret 30-second passages in both directions with structure, accuracy, and complete sentences before adding notes.

column476: Represent place assimilation of n, s before voiced consonants, and sounds such as [ɲ ʎ ʝ tʃ] in context.

column485: Evaluate arguments in public controversies over anglicisms, inclusive language, and dequeísmo, distinguishing descriptive claims from prescriptive ones.

Cumulative exam on the whole grade (listening, reading, use of language, speaking, writing), weighted toward the learner's weak-spot items and the level's key structures. Pass mark 80%; free retake after targeted repair. A pass unlocks the next grade.
